summary:
South Chungcheong Province stands under South Korea's national framework, which carries the country's criminal law, legal gender recognition rules, document policy and protection machinery. The province's own documented signal concerns students rather than visitors. Its student human-rights ordinance, enacted on 10 July 2020, contains Article 15, covering gender identity and sexual orientation. The provincial council voted to repeal the ordinance on 24 April 2024. The Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education, which enforces the ordinance, challenged the repeal at the Supreme Court on 13 May 2024 and obtained suspension of execution on 30 May 2024, so the ordinance remains in force while the case proceeds. The office argues that the repeal violates the Constitution and international human-rights treaties.

The ordinance's status is contested between sources. A reference article records that the province's ordinance was revoked in 2024, matching the 24 April 2024 council vote, while the Republic of Korea's submission to UN Special Procedures, dated 21 February 2025, states that the suspension of execution keeps it in effect. No region-specific rule on restroom access, healthcare, policing, hate-crime enforcement or violence in South Chungcheong was identified; for those matters the national assessment applies.
tangentialFactors: The province's ordinance belongs to a set of student human-rights ordinances adopted by provincial and metropolitan education authorities, in which the provisions on gender and sexual diversity have been the most contentious items. Repeal campaigns against such ordinances have been pursued through provincial councils and tested in the courts.
localsOnly: For students in South Chungcheong's schools, the ordinance remains operative pending the Supreme Court's decision, and the Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education is both its enforcing authority and a party to the dispute. The ordinance prohibits discrimination of students by gender, religion, nationality, disability, race and sexual orientation, with Article 15 addressing gender identity and sexual orientation. A repeal upheld by the court would remove those gender-identity and sexual-orientation protections from the province's student-rights framework.
outOfScopeNotes: Sources disagree on whether the ordinance is currently in force: a reference article records revocation in 2024, while the government's February 2025 submission to UN Special Procedures states that the 30 May 2024 suspension of execution leaves it in effect. The outcome of the Supreme Court challenge is unresolved in the available material. No documentation specific to South Chungcheong was identified on restroom access, healthcare access, hate-crime enforcement or violence. The same UN submission also addresses a parallel dispute in a different jurisdiction, which is not specific to this province.
